parts.label: Part I
parts.name: Extraversion (E) vs. Introversion (I)
parts.intro: This part explores where your attention naturally flows and what restores your energy: the outer world of people and activity, or the inner world of thoughts and reflection. Neither is better. Answer for the version of you that shows up on an ordinary week, not your best or worst day.

parts.label: Part II
parts.name: Sensing (S) vs. Intuition (N)
parts.intro: This part looks at the kind of information you trust and enjoy: concrete facts, details, and direct experience (Sensing), or patterns, possibilities, and meanings (Intuition).

subs.title: II-D. Trust in Experience vs. Hunches

parts.label: Part III
parts.name: Thinking (T) vs. Feeling (F)
parts.intro: This part explores how you make decisions: by impersonal logic, consistency, and cause-and-effect (Thinking), or by values, empathy, and the effect on people (Feeling). Everyone uses both; notice which one you reach for first.

parts.label: Part IV
parts.name: Judging (J) vs. Perceiving (P)
parts.intro: This part explores how you prefer to live in the outer world: planned, decided, and settled (Judging), or flexible, open, and adaptive (Perceiving). Judging is not "judgmental," and Perceiving is not "perceptive"; they describe structure versus openness.

parts.label: Part V
parts.name: Identity: Assertive (A) vs. Turbulent (T)
parts.intro: This optional fifth dimension explores emotional steadiness and self-assurance. Assertive types tend to be calm, confident, and resistant to stress; Turbulent types tend to be self-conscious, striving, and sensitive to stress, which often fuels high standards and growth. It is scored separately and does not change your four-letter type.

parts.label: Part VI
parts.name: Career, Work Style & Leadership
parts.intro: From here on, questions feed the place-fit scales rather than your four-letter type. There are no right answers; pick the option closest to you, even if none is perfect.

parts.label: Part VII
parts.name: Likes & Dislikes: Food, Hobbies, Entertainment & the Senses

parts.label: Part VIII
parts.name: Current Life Stage
parts.intro: These questions are about where you are right now. Questions about personal circumstances offer "Prefer not to say," which is never scored and never counts against you. Your answers help the test weigh family amenities, cost of living, and career ecosystems.

parts.label: Part IX
parts.name: Values, Civic Outlook & Spiritual Orientation
parts.intro: This part asks about values and worldview in plain, non-partisan language. No party names are used and no answer is better than another. Civic answers feed a single Civic Climate scale running from Traditional-leaning (low) through Center/Mixed (middle) to Progressive-leaning (high), so the test can suggest places where your outlook is common and you would feel at home. If you would rather not answer a question here, choose its "Prefer not to say" option where one is offered, or simply skip it; neither is scored.

parts.label: Part XI
parts.name: Social Energy & Relationships
parts.intro: Part I measured introversion and extraversion as a type. This part asks about the practical social life you want a place to support: how often you see people, how you meet them, and how close you want your neighbors.

subs.title: XI-C. Depth vs. Breadth of Relationships

parts.label: Part XIII
parts.name: Physical Environment: Climate, Landscape, Density & Cost
parts.intro: This part is the backbone of your location match. Answer for where you would thrive day-to-day for years, not where you would like to vacation for a week.

parts.label: Part XIV
parts.name: Community & Subculture Fit
parts.intro: The best place for you is not only a climate and a density; it is a tribe. These questions identify the subcultures you would thrive in. Many answers add points to Subculture Tags, which give bonus points to locations known for that scene.

parts.label: Part XV
parts.name: Dealbreakers & Must-Haves
parts.intro: These final questions are filters, not preferences. Answer "dealbreaker" or "must-have" only if you truly would refuse a place that fails the test. Each dealbreaker removes locations from consideration before scoring (see Step 6 of the Scoring Methodology). The last two questions set your top priorities, which double or increase the weight of certain scales.

questions.t: You arrive at a friend's birthday dinner and realize you know only the host, who is busy in the kitchen. What do you most likely do in the first ten minutes?
o: Check out the bookshelf, the playlist, or your phone until someone approaches you.
Offer to help the host in the kitchen so you have a task and a familiar face.
Find one person standing alone and start a quiet conversation with them.
Walk up to the liveliest cluster and introduce yourself with a joke about the parking situation.

questions.t: A new neighbor moves in across the hall. A week passes and you have not met. What happens next?
o: You knock with a plate of cookies or a six-pack and a big welcome.
You say hello the next time you happen to cross paths in the hallway.
You wait for them to introduce themselves; it feels presumptuous to intrude.
You will probably nod at each other for a year without learning names, and that is fine.

questions.t: At a conference coffee break, the person next to you in line is wearing a badge from a company you admire. You:
o: Ask them about their work immediately and swap contact info before the coffee is poured.
Make a light comment about the coffee and see whether they want to chat.
Think of a good opener but let the moment pass while you rehearse it.
Enjoy the break as a rare quiet moment and leave them to theirs.

questions.t: You are new in town and want friends. Which plan sounds most like you?
o: Join three clubs at once, say yes to every invitation, and host a housewarming within the month.
Join one recurring group (a run club, a trivia team) and let friendships form slowly.
Reconnect online with an acquaintance who lives nearby and meet them one-on-one.
Settle in first; friends will come through work or chance, and solitude is not a problem in the meantime.

questions.t: Your phone rings with an unknown local number. You:
o: Silence it and text back later, if at all; unscheduled calls feel intrusive.
Let it go to voicemail and listen afterwards.
Pick up cheerfully; it could be anything interesting.

questions.t: In a ride-share, the driver seems open to conversation. You:
o: Put your headphones in as soon as you sit down.
Give friendly but short answers that signal you would rather rest.
Chat politely for a few minutes, then settle into a comfortable quiet.
Learn their life story, their favorite taco spot, and their opinion on the local sports team.

questions.t: How do you usually make plans with friends?
o: I am the organizer: group chats, reservations, the whole thing.
I suggest plans sometimes, but I am just as happy when someone else takes charge.
I usually respond to invitations rather than send them.
People who know me know they will need to reach out; I rarely initiate.

questions.t: "I find it easy to start conversations with strangers."
Something wonderful happens: you get the job, the apartment, the yes. Your first instinct is to:
o: Call or text five people immediately and maybe post about it.
Tell your closest person right away and others over the next few days.
Sit with it privately for a while before telling anyone.
Keep it mostly to yourself; people will find out eventually.

questions.t: During a meeting or class discussion, you tend to:
o: Think out loud; my ideas get clearer as I say them.
Speak up once I have a reasonably formed point.
Speak only when I have something polished or when asked directly.
Contribute mostly in writing afterward, where I can be precise.

questions.t: Friends would describe your facial expressions and body language as:
o: An open book; you always know what I am feeling.
Generally readable, especially when I am excited.
Calm and somewhat hard to read.
A poker face; people are often surprised by what I was actually thinking.

questions.t: When telling a story at a gathering, you:
o: Act out the voices, use your hands, and build to a big punchline.
Tell it with energy, but keep it reasonably short.
Prefer to tell stories to one or two people, not the whole table.
Rarely tell stories in groups; you would rather listen to others'.

questions.t: Your speaking volume, according to the people around you, is:
o: Often a notch louder than everyone else's.
Normal, rising when I get passionate.
So quiet that people sometimes ask me to repeat myself.

questions.t: You are frustrated with a project at work. Coworkers are most likely to know because:
o: I will tell them, loudly, probably with a dramatic sigh.
I will vent to one trusted colleague.
They may notice I have gone quiet.
They will not know; I process it alone.

questions.t: "People usually know what I am thinking without my having to explain it."
When you have an opinion about a film you just watched with a group, you:
o: Share it before the credits finish rolling.
Share it once the conversation turns to the film.
Wait to hear what others think, then add a few thoughts.
Keep it to yourself unless someone asks; you are still digesting it.

questions.t: Your ideal Saturday night is:
o: A night in alone or with a partner, a project, and no plans.
A long dinner with one or two close friends.
A dinner for six to eight with good friends and a couple of new faces.
A packed house party where you bounce between rooms and meet new people.

questions.t: At a wedding reception, where are you at 10 p.m.?
o: In the middle of the dance floor, pulling others in.
Floating between tables, catching up with different people.
At a quieter table in a deep conversation with one person.
Already home or about to slip out without a big goodbye.

questions.t: A colleague invites you to a 40-person happy hour or a 4-person lunch. You prefer:
o: Neither; I would rather eat at my desk with a podcast.
The lunch, where conversation can go somewhere.
The happy hour, but I would leave after an hour.

questions.t: You win two tickets to a stadium concert with 50,000 people. Your reaction:
o: Thrilled; the crowd energy is half the point.
Excited, though I will plan an exit strategy for the crush.
Mixed; I would rather see the artist in a small venue.
I would probably give the tickets away.

questions.t: On a group trip with ten friends, you most enjoy:
o: Early mornings alone before everyone wakes up.
Splitting off with one or two people for most of the day.
A mix of group time and smaller outings.
Big group meals and activities where everyone is together.

questions.t: Working in an open-plan office with constant chatter feels:
o: Fine most days, with headphones on hand.
Draining; I need regular escapes to a quiet room.
Nearly unbearable; I do my real work after everyone leaves.

questions.t: How many people would you call good friends, people you would phone in a crisis?
o: More than fifteen; I have a big, overlapping web.
One or two, and that feels like plenty.

questions.t: "I feel more like myself in a crowd than when I am alone."
After a demanding week, which recharge sounds best?
o: A night out with friends: music, laughter, maybe dancing.
A relaxed dinner with a few people I love.
A solo walk, a book, and a long bath.
A whole weekend with no obligations and almost no talking.

questions.t: You have spent eight hours at an all-day workshop with constant group activities. How do you feel at 5 p.m.?
o: Wrung out; I may cancel my evening plans.
Done; I need quiet before I can talk to anyone else.
Pleasantly tired but social enough for dinner.
Wired and ready to grab drinks with the group.

questions.t: You are home alone for an unexpected free weekend. By Sunday afternoon you feel:
o: Blissful; I wish it were three days long.
Rested but ready to see people.
Restless and lonely; I would have made plans by Saturday.

questions.t: When you are stuck on a problem, what helps most?
o: Talking it through with whoever will listen.
Bouncing it off one smart friend.
Going for a walk alone and thinking.
Writing about it privately until it resolves.

questions.t: On a long solo drive or flight, you mostly:
o: Make phone calls or chat with seatmates.
Listen to talk radio or conversational podcasts, which feel like company.
Listen to music and let my mind wander.
Enjoy the silence; it is restful in a way daily life is not.

questions.t: How do you feel when plans with friends get cancelled at the last minute?
o: Disappointed; I start texting others to fill the gap.
A little let down, but I will find something to do.
Openly relieved; cancelled plans are one of life's small joys.

questions.t: If you had to work from home permanently with no in-person colleagues, you would:
o: Feel isolated quickly and seek out coworking spaces or cafes daily.
Like it, but need regular social plans to balance it.
Thrive; I would see friends on my own terms.

questions.t: "Long stretches of time alone leave me feeling recharged rather than restless."
When you walk into a room, what do you notice first?
o: The people: who is here, who is talking, where the energy is.
The general mood of the room.
The layout, the exits, a quiet corner.
My own thoughts; I may not notice much at all at first.

questions.t: Someone asks you a complex question in conversation. You:
o: Ask whether I can get back to them once I have thought it over.
Pause noticeably to think before answering.
Answer fairly quickly with a reasonable take.
Answer right away and refine as I go.

questions.t: Interruptions while you are working tend to:
o: Genuinely derail me; I guard my focus time closely.
Break my concentration, and I need a few minutes to get back in.
Be welcome; a quick chat breaks up the monotony.

questions.t: Your mind at rest, say lying in bed before sleep, is usually:
o: Replaying conversations and planning tomorrow's social plans.
A mix of to-do lists and people.
Wandering through ideas, memories, and imaginary scenarios.
A rich private world that feels as real as the outer one.

questions.t: You learn about a fascinating new topic. Your instinct is to:
o: Keep it as a private interest that I rarely discuss.
Go deeper alone first: read, watch, absorb.
Bring it up next time it fits the conversation.

questions.t: In a brainstorm session, you are most useful:
o: In a follow-up email the next day, once I have had time to think.
Taking notes and offering a few well-considered ideas at the end.
In the room, building on others' ideas out loud.
At the whiteboard, generating ideas rapid-fire with the group.

questions.t: You prefer to communicate important news by:
o: Phone or in person; it is more alive.
A thoughtful message they can read when ready.
Email or letter where I can choose every word.

questions.t: "I often realize what I think only after I have said it out loud."
You are an introvert-ish person's plus-one at their office holiday party. They vanish to the restroom for 20 minutes. You:
o: Have made three new friends and booked a pickleball date by the time they return.
Hold a pleasant conversation with whoever is nearby.
Hover by the snack table and look busy.
Text them "where are you??" and step outside for air.

questions.t: You are offered a promotion that doubles your public-facing work (presentations, client dinners, events) for a 15% raise. You:
o: Accept eagerly; the people side is the best part.
Accept, knowing I will need to protect some quiet time.
Hesitate and negotiate to keep part of my current behind-the-scenes role.
Decline; the raise is not worth the drain.

questions.t: Your power goes out for a full evening. The neighbors start gathering on the stoop with candles and drinks. You:
o: Stay in; a blackout is a perfect excuse for solitude.
Wave, chat briefly, and enjoy the candlelit quiet inside.
Join for an hour, then go back inside.
Bring out chairs and snacks; this is a block party now.

questions.t: At a silent meditation retreat, the hardest part for you would be:
o: The silence; not talking for days sounds like torture.
The silence at first, though I could adjust.
Sitting still physically; the silence would be lovely.
Leaving at the end and returning to noise.

questions.t: You are seated next to a stranger on a five-hour flight who wants to talk the entire time. You feel:
o: Trapped; I would invent an urgent nap.
Polite but quietly desperate for my book.
Fine for an hour, then ready for a movie.
Delighted; a new friend at 30,000 feet.

questions.t: A friend suggests a two-week solo trek through a remote national park with almost no human contact. Your gut says:
o: Intriguing, if I could check in by phone occasionally.
Maybe with a group tour instead.
No way; I would want companions.

questions.t: Which comment from a friend would feel most accurate?
o: "I feel like I am still getting to know you after years."
"You are always fun to have around."
"You are the glue of our friend group."

questions.t: "After a great party, I often feel more energized than when I arrived."
A friend describes a new restaurant. Which description makes you want to go?
o: "The brisket is smoked for 14 hours, the portions are huge, and it is $18 with two sides."
"It has a cool vibe, like a speakeasy crossed with a family reunion."
"It feels like the beginning of something; this whole block is about to change."

questions.t: You are assembling a new bookshelf. You:
o: Get halfway, realize you could redesign it to be better, and modify it.
Look at the picture on the box and figure it out as you go.
Skim the instructions, then follow them where it matters.
Lay out every piece, count the screws, and follow the instructions step by step.

questions.t: After a vacation, what do you remember most vividly?
o: The ideas and insights it sparked about how I want to live.
The overall feeling of the trip and what it meant to me.
The activities we did and the places we went, in order.
Specific sensory details: the smell of the market, the texture of the sand, the exact meal.

questions.t: When reading a news article, you most want:
o: Hard numbers, dates, names, and quotes.
A clear summary of what happened.
Speculation about what it means for the future.

questions.t: You notice when a coworker:
o: Gets a haircut or wears new shoes, immediately.
Changes something significant about their appearance.
Seems to be in a different mood than usual.
Is going through a broader life shift, often before they mention it.

questions.t: When giving directions, you say:
o: "Go 0.4 miles, turn left at the Shell station, it is the third house with the green door."
"Left at the gas station, then look for the green door."
"Head toward the river and you will see it, sort of on the hill."
"Just put it in your phone; I am terrible with directions."

questions.t: Which compliment pleases you most?
"I would rather perfect a method that works than invent a new one."
You spend a spare hour daydreaming. What are you thinking about?
o: I do not really daydream; I would rather do something.
What I will cook for dinner or what I need to fix this weekend.
Where I might be in five years.
Entire alternate lives, inventions, or worlds.

questions.t: A coworker pitches a radical new way of doing your team's main process. Your first reaction is:
o: "Yes! And while we are at it, let us rethink the whole department."
"Show me data from a pilot first."
"What is wrong with the way it works now?"

questions.t: Which statement fits you best?
o: I live largely in the future; the present is mostly a launch pad.
Keep one eye on where things are heading.
Focus on what is right in front of you and handle it well.
Enjoy the moment; tomorrow will take care of itself.

questions.t: When you plan a garden, you think mostly about:
o: Soil, sunlight hours, spacing, and which tomato variety yields best.
Which plants I like and what grows well here.
How it will look and feel in three summers.
Whether the garden could become a community space, a business, or an art project.

questions.t: Your relationship with nostalgia and history:
o: The past is interesting only as a pattern that predicts the future.
I am more interested in what is coming than what has been.
I like remembering good times, but mostly I am in the present.
I treasure traditions and how things have always been done.

questions.t: You are handed a vague assignment: "Make the onboarding experience better." You:
o: Ask for specific metrics and current pain points before starting.
Interview a few new hires to find concrete problems.
Sketch three different visions of what onboarding could be.
Question whether onboarding should exist in its current form at all.

questions.t: "I often get so absorbed in imagining possibilities that I miss what is happening around me."
You inherit a run-down cabin. Your first weekend there, you:
o: Dream up five wildly different uses for it, from artist residency to tiny resort.
Imagine what it could become with the right vision.
Clean it up and make it usable right away.
Inspect the roof, plumbing, and wiring and write a repair list.

questions.t: Which class sounds most appealing?
o: Philosophy of mind or theoretical physics.

questions.t: You explain a concept to a friend. You naturally use:
o: A theory or framework that ties it to other concepts.

questions.t: Which book would you pick for a long flight?
o: Speculative science fiction or a book of big ideas.
A literary novel full of symbolism.
A biography or a well-researched history.
A practical how-to guide or a detailed true-crime account.

questions.t: When you hear a song for the first time, you notice:
o: The instruments, production quality, and how it sounds.
The beat and whether it is catchy.
The mood and what it reminds me of.
The hidden meaning in the lyrics and what the artist is really saying.

questions.t: Talk of "the meaning of life" makes you:
o: Restless; let us talk about something real.
Mildly interested for a few minutes.
Light up; I could do this until 3 a.m.

questions.t: In a museum, you spend the most time:
o: At pieces that make you question something.
At pieces that make you feel something.
Reading the placards about when and how things were made.
At exhibits with real artifacts you can examine up close.

questions.t: Your attitude toward instruction manuals:
o: I read them thoroughly before starting.
I rarely look; I prefer to explore.
I often find a use for the product the manual never mentions.

questions.t: "Facts speak for themselves; I distrust interpretations."
Choosing a contractor, you rely most on:
o: A gut feeling I cannot fully explain.
My overall impression of them after a conversation.
Reviews and a solid written quote.
Licenses, references, and their track record on similar jobs.

questions.t: You have a strong hunch a friend's new partner is not right for them, but you cannot point to evidence. You:
o: Trust it completely; my hunches are usually right.
Trust it enough to stay alert and maybe mention it gently.
Keep an eye out for concrete warning signs.
Dismiss it; hunches without facts are not worth much.

questions.t: When cooking, you:
o: Invent dishes from whatever is in the fridge.
Follow recipes but adjust seasoning to taste.
Follow recipes exactly and measure everything.

questions.t: You learned your most useful skills by:
o: Making unexpected connections between unrelated fields.

questions.t: When a friend tells you about a problem, you notice:
o: Exactly what happened and who said what.
The practical facts of the situation.
The pattern; this is the third time something like this has happened.
What it says about their deeper life story.

questions.t: Your workspace or desk is usually decorated with:
o: Odd collections of things that mean something only to me.
A few practical items and a photo or two.

questions.t: A stock everyone is talking about doubles in a week. You:
o: Try to spot the next idea before it becomes the conversation.
Think about where the industry is going.
Wait to see whether the trend holds.
Look at the company's actual revenue and balance sheet.

questions.t: "I trust what I can see, touch, and measure more than what I sense intuitively."
Your writing style (emails, texts, notes) tends to be:
o: Literal and direct: who, what, when, where.
Full of tangents and connections that excite me even if they confuse others.

questions.t: As a child, your favorite play was:
o: Building things, sports, or anything hands-on.
Inventing entire worlds, languages, or secret societies.

questions.t: Someone says, "The meeting was a train wreck." You picture:
o: Specific things that went wrong in the meeting.
Why meetings in this company keep derailing; the metaphor suggests a whole theory.

questions.t: Which TV show would you most likely binge?
o: A home-renovation or cooking competition show.
A character-driven drama with layered meaning.
A mind-bending series with twists, time loops, and theories online.

questions.t: A friend says, "What if cities had no cars at all?" You:
o: Point out the practical problems: deliveries, emergency vehicles, disability access.
Discuss which existing car-free streets work well.
Imagine what daily life would feel like.
Spin out a whole redesigned society around the idea.

questions.t: When you shop for clothes, you focus on:
o: Unusual combinations that nobody else would think of.
How it expresses my mood or identity.

questions.t: Repetitive, routine tasks (filing, data entry, folding laundry):
o: Are satisfying; I like the rhythm.
Are fine; I put on music and get it done.
Make me feel like my brain is atrophying.

questions.t: "I am often called a dreamer."
You are on a hike and get slightly lost. Your instinct is to:
o: Retrace your steps exactly to the last trail marker you remember.
Check the map and the position of the sun.
Enjoy being lost for a bit; maybe there is something cool out here.

questions.t: You are planning a surprise party. What part do you enjoy most?
o: Imagining how the party could become an annual tradition with its own lore.
Designing the theme and the emotional moment of the reveal.

questions.t: A friend asks what you think of their abstract painting. You say:
o: "The colors are nice and the brushwork is clean."
"I like it; what is it of?"
"It reminds me of a dream I had about the ocean and memory."

questions.t: You are given a free afternoon in an unfamiliar city. You:
o: Ride a random bus line to the end to see what is there.
Visit the top-rated attraction and the best-reviewed lunch spot.

questions.t: Your memory is best for:
Your boss says the company will "pivot to the future." Your reaction:
o: "I already have six ideas for what the future should be."
"Exciting; I wonder where we are heading."
"I will wait for the actual plan."

questions.t: Which object would you rather receive as a gift?
o: A strange antique with a mysterious backstory.
A beautiful journal or an art print.
A useful gadget I had been eyeing.
A high-quality cast-iron pan or a well-made tool.

questions.t: "I am more interested in what could be than in what is."
Your company must lay off one of two employees. One is slightly more productive; the other is a single parent who has been there ten years. Your instinct says:
o: Keep the more productive employee; the decision has to be based on performance.
Lean toward performance, but look for ways to soften the blow.
Weigh the human impact heavily; ten years of loyalty matters.
Keep the single parent; I could not live with the alternative.

questions.t: Buying a car, what tips the decision?
o: Reliability ratings, total cost of ownership, and resale value.
Specs and price, plus a test drive.
How it feels to drive and what it says about me.
Whether my family loves it and it feels "right."

questions.t: A friend asks you to be a reference for a job you think they are not qualified for. You:
o: Agree enthusiastically; supporting friends comes first.
Agree and focus on their strengths and character.
Agree, but speak only to the skills I can genuinely vouch for.

questions.t: When choosing between two job offers, the deciding factor is most likely:
o: Salary, growth trajectory, and objective career value.
Pay and responsibilities, with culture as a tiebreaker.
The people I would work with and how I felt in the interview.
Which mission I believe in and which choice feels true to who I am.

questions.t: "Fairness means applying the same rules to everyone, regardless of circumstances."
You are on a jury. The defendant is clearly guilty by law, but you find their motives deeply sympathetic. You:
o: Consider whether justice is better served by mercy.
Vote guilty, but hope for a lenient sentence.
Vote guilty; the law is the law.

questions.t: Picking a restaurant for a group, you prioritize:
o: The objectively best-reviewed option within budget.
Good food at a convenient location.
A place where everyone will feel comfortable.
Whatever the person having the hardest week would enjoy most.

questions.t: "When making a hard decision, I trust my head more than my heart."
A friend shows you a business plan with a fatal flaw. You:
o: Encourage them; maybe they will figure it out, and they seem so excited.
Start with what is good, then gently raise the concern.
Ask questions that lead them to find the flaw themselves.
Point out the flaw right away, clearly and specifically.

questions.t: Your partner asks if their new haircut looks good. It does not. You say:
o: "I love it!" Their happiness matters more than my opinion.
"You look great; it might just need a little time to settle."
"It is different; give me a day to get used to it."
"Honestly, not my favorite. The old one suited you better."

questions.t: Receiving criticism at work, you prefer:
o: Blunt and direct; do not waste time softening it.
Balanced with acknowledgment of what went well.
Delivered privately and kindly, with clear care for me as a person.

questions.t: Someone at a dinner party states a "fact" that is clearly wrong. You:
o: Correct them lightly, maybe with a joke.
Let it go unless it really matters.
Let it go; embarrassing them is not worth it.

questions.t: "I would rather be respected than liked."
You manage someone who is kind and hardworking but consistently underperforms. You:
o: Put them on a formal improvement plan with clear metrics.
Have a frank talk about expectations and offer targeted training.
Try to understand what is going on in their life first.
Look for a role that fits their strengths better, even if it means reorganizing.

questions.t: In a debate, you care most about:
o: Winning the argument with airtight logic.

questions.t: A colleague cries in a meeting after their idea is rejected. You feel:
o: Uncomfortable; emotions do not belong in a business decision.
Sympathetic, but the decision should not change.
Concerned; I would check on them afterwards.
Moved, and I would want to revisit how we handled it.

questions.t: Watching a sad movie, you:
o: Analyze the plot holes and cinematography.
Feel a bit moved, but stay composed.
Tear up at the key moments.
Cry openly and think about it for days.

questions.t: A friend vents about a problem. You naturally:
o: Feel their pain almost as if it were mine.
Listen and reflect back how they must feel.
Ask whether they want advice or just to vent.
Offer solutions; that is the most useful thing I can do.

questions.t: Tension in a group you belong to:
o: Does not bother me much; disagreement is healthy.
Is fine if it is productive.
Makes me uneasy until it is resolved.
Physically stresses me; I work hard to restore harmony.

questions.t: You notice someone being left out at a party. You:
o: Spend most of the night making sure they are having a good time.
Make a point to include them.
Notice but assume they are fine.
Probably do not notice; I am in my own conversation.

questions.t: "I can usually sense how others are feeling, even when they hide it."
You must choose between a holiday with family who will be hurt if you do not come and a once-in-a-lifetime work trip. You:
o: Take the work trip; the opportunity cost is too high.
Take the trip and plan a special visit later.
Agonize, then probably go to the family holiday.
Go home; family feelings are not something to trade.

questions.t: When people describe you as "too sensitive" or "too blunt," it is usually:
o: Too blunt, and I am fine with that.
Too sensitive, and I am working on owning it as a strength.

questions.t: A charity appeal shows a photo of one hungry child; another shows a chart of a million people in need. Which moves you more?
o: The chart; scale is what matters.
Both equally, though the numbers convince me.
The photo, and I would donate immediately.

questions.t: What frustrates you more?
Which job would you find more satisfying?
o: Designing a more efficient supply chain.

questions.t: "Rules should bend for good reasons."
You catch a close friend in a small lie that hurts no one. You:
o: Call it out; honesty is non-negotiable.
Mention it lightly to show I noticed.
Let it go, but remember it.
Let it go; there was probably a reason.

questions.t: Which describes your moral reasoning best?
o: Context and relationships matter as much as principles.
What feels compassionate in the moment.

questions.t: When splitting a dinner bill, you prefer:
o: Quietly cover the friend who is short on money.
Split evenly; it is simpler and kinder.
Split evenly unless there is a big difference.
Everyone pays exactly what they ordered.

questions.t: "I find it easy to stay objective when people I care about are involved."
A rule at work seems pointless. You:
o: Ignore it if following it would hurt someone.
Ask how others feel about it before acting.
Follow it while documenting why it does not work.
Present a logical case for eliminating it.

questions.t: Your texts are usually:
o: Warm and expressive; I hate the idea of sounding cold.
Friendly, with exclamation points and emoji.
Clear, with occasional punctuation of warmth.

questions.t: In a heated argument with a loved one, you are most likely to say:
o: "I just want us to be okay."
"I feel hurt when you say that."

questions.t: When you compliment someone, you focus on:
o: How they made me or others feel.

questions.t: "Tact is overrated; people should just say what they mean."
You are asked to give a toast at a friend's wedding. Your toast is:
o: Witty and clever, with a well-crafted structure.
A few good stories and a clean ending.
So emotional that I may not get through it without crying.

questions.t: When a coworker pitches an idea you dislike, you say:
o: "Thank you for sharing this," and then raise concerns privately.
"I like the direction; what if we tweaked a few things?"
"I see some problems; can we stress-test it?"
"This will not work because of X, Y, and Z."

questions.t: People come to you mostly for:
A friend asks, "Do you think I made the right call quitting my job?" Your answer begins with:
o: "I am proud of you for listening to yourself."
"It depends on what your plan is now."
"Let us look at whether the numbers work."

questions.t: You find a wallet with $300 and an ID. You:
o: Return it and add a kind note.
Return it, imagining how relieved the owner will be.
Return it; it is the right thing to do.
Return it with everything; that is simply the rule.

questions.t: A self-driving car must choose between hitting one person or swerving into three. When you hear this dilemma you:
o: Calculate: one is fewer than three.
Think about which principle should govern the programming.
Feel uneasy about reducing people to numbers.
Reject the framing; the human cost is unbearable either way.

questions.t: Your elderly parent wants to keep driving, but their reflexes are slipping. You:
o: Present the safety data and insist they stop.
Have a long, gentle conversation about their independence.
Find a solution that preserves their dignity first, even if it takes time.

questions.t: A shelter dog you are fostering bites someone lightly. You:
o: Feel heartbroken and fight hard for the dog's second chance.
Worry about what will happen to the dog.
Report it, but advocate for an evaluation.
Report it and follow protocol exactly.

questions.t: If you had to describe your ideal leader, it would be:
Your teenager (or a young relative) wants to drop out of college to pursue music. You:
o: Ask what the dream means to them.
Suggest a compromise: finish the semester, then reassess.
Lay out the financial reality in a spreadsheet.

questions.t: You see a viral video of a stranger behaving badly. You:
o: Want to know the full context before judging.
Judge the behavior, not the person.
Feel bad for everyone involved, including them.
Worry about the pile-on and how they are coping.

questions.t: "Being right matters more to me than keeping the peace."
You are going on a week-long vacation. Your itinerary looks like:
o: A color-coded spreadsheet with reservations, times, and backup options.
Flights, lodging, and a few must-do activities booked; the rest loose.
Flights and the first night booked; we will figure it out.
A one-way ticket and a vague direction.

questions.t: Your calendar right now is:
o: Detailed down to gym sessions and grocery runs.
Work commitments and major social plans.
Sparse; I keep most things in my head.

questions.t: A friend texts on Friday at 6 p.m.: "Want to drive to the coast tonight?" You:
o: Decline; my weekend is already planned.
Consider it if I can rearrange things easily.
Say yes after a quick mental check.
Am already packing before I finish reading the message.

questions.t: When do you start a project due in three weeks?
o: Day one, with a schedule of milestones.
In a heroic burst the night before; pressure is my fuel.

questions.t: "I feel uneasy when I do not know what my week looks like."
You plan meals for the week by:
o: Deciding at 7 p.m. based on cravings, often with takeout.
A rotating meal plan with a shopping list organized by store aisle.

questions.t: A dinner reservation gets moved from 7:00 to 8:30. You feel:
o: Fine; more time to get ready.
Annoyed; it throws off my whole evening.

questions.t: Your relationship with to-do lists:
o: I make them daily and love crossing things off.
I use them for busy periods.
I make them and then lose them.
I do not make them; I deal with what is in front of me.

questions.t: Choosing an apartment, you:
o: Decide quickly once one meets my criteria; done is better than perfect.
See a handful, then choose within a few days.
Keep looking even after finding a good one, just in case.
Have trouble committing; what if something better comes up?

questions.t: At a restaurant with a giant menu, you:
o: Decide in under a minute, often the same dish as always.
Narrow it down quickly and choose.
Order last and still second-guess it when the food arrives.

questions.t: An unresolved question (Where will we live? What will I do next?) hanging over you feels:
o: Exciting; uncertainty means anything can happen.
Uncomfortable, but I can wait for more information.

questions.t: "Once I make a decision, I rarely revisit it."
In a group discussion that keeps going in circles, you:
o: Push for a vote so we can move on.
Summarize the options and suggest a decision.
Keep exploring; the best idea may not have come up yet.
Enjoy the tangents; that is where the good stuff is.

questions.t: Your career path so far has been:
o: A zigzag of reinventions that somehow makes sense in hindsight.
Mostly planned, with a few adjustments.
Planned since school, step by step.

questions.t: You are shopping for a gift. You:
o: Get distracted and buy something for myself instead.
Browse until something speaks to me.
Have a short list and pick one.
Know exactly what to buy and where before leaving home.

questions.t: Rules and procedures, in general:
o: Make life smoother; I appreciate them.
Are useful most of the time.
Feel like cages; I find workarounds.

questions.t: Your closet is:
o: Organized chaos; I know where things are.
A chair covered in clothes counts as a closet.

questions.t: When you arrive at a hotel room, you:
o: Unpack completely into drawers on the first night.
Explode the suitcase across every surface within an hour.

questions.t: The dishes after dinner:
o: Are done before I sit down for the evening.
Are done when there are no clean ones left.

questions.t: "A messy space makes it hard for me to think."
Your email inbox right now has:
o: Thousands. It is fine. It is fine.
Hundreds, but the important ones are handled.

questions.t: Your car (or bag) contains:
o: Receipts, wrappers, and a mystery sweatshirt.
Enough random stuff to survive a week off-grid.

questions.t: When you have guests coming over, you clean:
o: The day before, thoroughly, with a checklist.
In a frantic 20-minute sprint before the doorbell rings.
Not at all; they are coming to see me, not my floors.

questions.t: Your digital files are:
o: In a nested folder system with clear naming conventions.
On the desktop, but I can search.
Scattered across five devices and three cloud services.

questions.t: A deadline is:
o: A firm commitment; I usually finish early.
A target I hit on time.
A strong suggestion that I sometimes push.
The moment I actually begin working.

questions.t: You work best:
o: On whatever is most exciting right now, with ten projects half-done.
Switching among several tasks as my interest shifts.
On a few tasks with clear priorities.
On one task at a time, finished before moving on.

questions.t: Your boss changes the project's direction halfway through. You:
o: Love it; change keeps things interesting.
Feel frustrated; the plan was working.

questions.t: "I get more done when I have a clear schedule than when I go with the flow."
When starting something new (a hobby, a job), you:
o: Research thoroughly and create a plan.
Jump in and learn as I go.
Jump in, switch approaches three times, and end up somewhere unexpected.

questions.t: Your ideal job structure:
o: Clear hours, clear expectations, predictable workflow.
Total autonomy; no two days alike.

questions.t: How do you feel about "winging it" in a presentation?
o: I do my best work improvising.

questions.t: When a project ends, you:
o: Have already mentally moved on before it ended.
Move on, leaving a few loose ends.
Tie up loose ends and move on.
Write a wrap-up document and archive everything.

questions.t: Your morning routine:
o: Does not exist; every morning is a fresh adventure.
Is the same every day, timed to the minute.

questions.t: A street fair appears unexpectedly on your way to run errands. You:
o: Stick to my errands; I can come back another time.
Make a quick detour if I have time.
Wander through and do the errands later.

questions.t: "I enjoy surprises, even when they disrupt my plans."
Your approach to money is:
o: I deal with money when I have to.
I keep a rough sense of what is in the account.

questions.t: When you have a free weekend, by Friday you have:
o: Nothing, and I like it that way.
A few ideas but nothing fixed.
One or two plans and some open time.

questions.t: Your packing for a trip happens:
o: In the ten minutes before the ride arrives, and I always forget something.
Days in advance, from a reusable checklist.

questions.t: Your favorite type of weekend activity:
o: Recurring commitments: my weekly game, class, or volunteer shift.
Whatever my friends are up to.
Something I have never done before, decided that morning.

questions.t: When others are late:
o: It bothers me a lot; time is respect.

questions.t: Your flight is cancelled and the next one is tomorrow. You:
o: Immediately rebook, book a hotel, and rework tomorrow's schedule.
Rebook and figure out the rest within the hour.
Shrug and explore the city for the night.
Consider whether I even need to go; maybe a road trip instead?

questions.t: You are given a year off with full pay. On day one, you:
o: Sleep in and see where it goes.

questions.t: A friend proposes moving in together in two weeks. You:
o: Have already started looking at places.
Are open; we will figure it out.
Need a detailed plan: lease, budget, chores chart.

questions.t: Choosing what to watch on a streaming service:
o: I start four shows and finish none.
I pick from my list fairly quickly.
I have a queue and watch it in order.

questions.t: A board game with a 40-page rulebook:
o: I make up house rules by turn three.
I prefer someone explain it as we go.
I skim it and look things up as needed.
I read it all before we play.

questions.t: When your plans fall through, you:
o: Feel unsettled until I have a new plan.
Make a new plan fairly quickly.
Feel relieved; I prefer an empty slate.

questions.t: Your attitude toward long-term commitments (mortgages, contracts, multi-year leases):
o: Comforting; I like knowing where I stand.
Fine if the terms are right.
Deeply uncomfortable; I like my exits open.

questions.t: "I prefer to keep my options open rather than settle things early."
After a job interview, you usually:
o: Feel confident I did well and move on.
Replay a moment or two, but feel okay overall.
Replay several answers and wish I had said them differently.
Lose sleep over every word for days.

questions.t: When someone compliments your work, you:
o: Deflect and point out what could be better.
Accept it, with a little modesty.
Say thank you and believe it.

questions.t: "I rarely worry about what other people think of me."
You make a visible mistake at work. Afterward you:
o: Fix it, learn from it, and let it go.
Feel embarrassed briefly, then let it go.
Feel bad for the rest of the day.
Feel bad for weeks and work twice as hard to make up for it.

questions.t: Comparing yourself to peers on social media makes you:
o: Anxious enough that I limit my exposure.
Indifferent; I run my own race.

questions.t: Your inner voice is mostly:
o: Harsh; I would never talk to a friend that way.

questions.t: Your mood across an ordinary week is:
A sudden unexpected bill of $1,000 arrives. You:
o: Feel a jolt, then make a plan.
Spiral into what-ifs about my finances overall.

questions.t: "I often feel that I need to improve myself."
Before a big event (presentation, wedding, competition), you sleep:
When things are going well, you:
o: Feel sure something bad is coming.
Wait for the other shoe to drop.

questions.t: A friend does not text back for two days. You:
o: Reread our last conversation several times.
Wonder if I said something wrong.
Think nothing of it until day three.

questions.t: A major goal fails (rejected application, failed business). You:
o: Bounce back quickly and try again.
Take a short break, then regroup.
Need a long time to recover my confidence.
Question whether I should try at all anymore.

questions.t: Your standards for yourself are:
o: Very high; I push myself hard.
High, but I can let things go.
Reasonable; good enough is often good enough.

questions.t: "I am satisfied with who I am right now."
When you achieve something big, the feeling lasts:
o: A long time; I savor it.
A day or two before I focus on the next thing.
Minutes; then I see what is still missing.

questions.t: You are asked to lead something you have never done before. You:
o: Say yes confidently; I will figure it out.
Hesitate and doubt whether I am the right person.
Suggest someone else who would be "better."

questions.t: Your relationship with regret:
o: A few regrets, at peace with them.
I rarely feel it; every choice taught me something.

questions.t: A stranger criticizes you harshly online. You:
o: Feel a sting and move on.
Think about it for the rest of the day.
Draft five responses and maybe delete my post.

questions.t: You are about to walk into a room full of people more accomplished than you. You feel:
o: Excited to meet them as equals.

questions.t: "When something goes wrong, my first thought is that it is my fault."
Your doctor says a test result needs a follow-up. You:
o: Schedule it calmly and do not dwell.
Feel some concern but stay level.
Assume the worst until the follow-up.

questions.t: You realize mid-presentation that a slide has a typo. You:
o: Lose my rhythm for a minute.
Think about the typo for the rest of the talk.

questions.t: Your general outlook on the next five years is:
If money were equal across all options, which work would you choose?
o: Building software, data systems, or hardware products.
Caring for patients or improving people's health.
Making art, music, film, writing, or design.
Building, repairing, or operating physical things: construction, machinery, energy, manufacturing.
Managing money, deals, investments, or risk.

questions.t: Which headline about you would make you proudest?
o: "Local founder's app reaches a million users."
"Public servant's policy cuts commute times citywide."
"Professor's research changes how we understand memory."
"Family farm wins regional award for sustainable practices."

questions.t: At a career fair, which booth do you walk to first?
o: The federal agency or city government booth.
The investment bank or insurance firm.
The hotel group, restaurant group, or tourism board.

questions.t: Which task would you happily do for a full afternoon?
o: Debugging code until it finally runs.
Writing a policy memo that could influence a law.
Designing a poster, editing a video, or composing a track.
Teaching a class of curious students.
Planning an unforgettable event for 200 guests.

questions.t: Which workplace sounds most like home?
o: A startup loft with whiteboards and standing desks.
A university campus with old trees and a library.
A clinic or lab with a clear mission.
A workshop, job site, or factory floor.
A trading floor or a polished downtown office tower.

questions.t: Your dream side hustle would be:
o: A small farm stand, orchard, or apiary.
Freelance illustration, photography, or music gigs.
Consulting on budgets and investments for friends.
Building apps or automations on weekends.

questions.t: Where is your current or intended work actually done?
o: Fully remote; I could do it from almost anywhere with internet.
Hybrid; I need an office within reach a few days a week.
On-site in a specific industry hub.
Wherever the customers, patients, or job sites are; it is local by nature.
Not working for pay right now or retired.

questions.t: Which of these communities would you most like to be part of professionally?
o: Developers and founders at meetups and hackathons.
Policy wonks, nonprofit staff, and public servants.

questions.t: Your ideal commute is:
o: A walk or bike ride through a busy neighborhood.
A short train or bus ride with a book.
Down the hall to my home office or out to the barn.

questions.t: The ideal size of the organization you work for:
o: A global company with tens of thousands of employees.
A small business or startup of under 50 people.
Just me, or me plus a partner.

questions.t: The pace of your ideal workday:
o: Fast and intense: deadlines, deals, adrenaline.
Slow and unhurried, with long lunches.

questions.t: "I would trade a higher salary for a shorter workweek and more free time."
How important is it that your industry has many employers in the same city, so you can switch jobs without moving?
o: Essential; I want a deep job market.
Not important; I am loyal or self-employed.
Irrelevant; I am remote or not working.

questions.t: Which after-work culture appeals to you most?
o: Team trivia or a company softball league.
Everyone goes home to their families.
Colleagues who go hiking or skiing together.

questions.t: Dress code you would prefer:
o: Boots and work clothes, or whatever I want.

questions.t: How do you feel about a workplace that blends work and personal identity (mission-driven, social-justice focused, "we are a family")?
o: Love it; my work should reflect my values.
I prefer clear boundaries; work is work.

questions.t: In a group project with no assigned leader, you:
o: Take charge immediately and assign roles.
Step up if no one else does.
Prefer to be a strong second-in-command.
Do my part well and let others steer.

questions.t: Your ideal relationship with a boss:
o: I would rather be the boss.
A mentor who gives me autonomy.
A clear leader who sets direction.
A collaborative peer more than a boss.

questions.t: When a team you lead misses a goal, you:
o: Analyze the failure and redesign the process.
Take responsibility publicly and fix it privately.
Check in on morale before anything else.
Hand leadership to someone better suited.

questions.t: Which leadership style do you admire most?
You are offered a choice of roles on a big project. You take:
o: Lead specialist, the expert others rely on.
Independent contributor on a piece I can own entirely.

questions.t: "I would rather be a big fish in a small pond than a small fish in a big pond."
How do you feel about climbing a corporate ladder?
o: Very motivated; title and scope matter to me.
Indifferent; I care about the work itself.
Allergic; I would rather build something of my own or opt out.

questions.t: Your ideal level of public visibility at work:
o: Known and respected in my field.

questions.t: What matters most in your next job?
How much career risk are you comfortable with?
o: A lot; I would bet on a startup or my own business.
Little; I value a reliable paycheck.

questions.t: Your view on unions and skilled trades:
o: I am in, or would love to be in, a skilled trade.
I respect them and know people in them.
I have little connection to that world.

questions.t: Which would you most like to be known for professionally?
"I want a job I can leave at the office at 5 p.m."
Which work problem would excite you most?
o: Scaling a product from a thousand users to a million.
Getting a bill passed or a program funded.
Opening a restaurant in a neighborhood that needs one.

questions.t: Your relationship with competition at work:
o: I thrive on it; rankings motivate me.
A little friendly competition is healthy.

questions.t: Which of these would you happily teach others?
How do you feel about seasonal work rhythms (busy summers, quiet winters, or vice versa) like those in tourism or agriculture towns?
o: Love it; it matches my energy.

questions.t: Your dream title in ten years:
o: Director of a public agency or nonprofit.
Chief of Medicine or head nurse.
Owner of a respected local business.

questions.t: When work and family conflict, you most often:
o: Try to balance, leaning toward work.
Try to balance, leaning toward family.
Prioritize family; work is how I fund my life.

questions.t: Which would make you quit a job?
Which describes your ideal professional reputation in your community?
o: Known by name at the local hardware store and diner.
Not known at all; I like anonymity.

questions.t: Your ideal Friday dinner:
o: A tasting menu at a chef-driven restaurant I booked weeks ago.
A hole-in-the-wall taqueria, pho shop, or dumpling house someone swears by.
A backyard barbecue or fish fry with neighbors.
A home-cooked meal from my own garden or the farmers market.

questions.t: How adventurous are you with food?
o: I will try anything: insects, offal, the spiciest thing on the menu.
I love trying new cuisines, within reason.
I like a few favorites and branch out occasionally.
I know what I like, and I order it every time.

questions.t: Which food scene would make you happiest to live near?
o: Dozens of immigrant-run restaurants from every continent.
Classic regional cooking: barbecue, Southern, Tex-Mex, Cajun, or New England seafood.
Farm-to-table cafes and a great Saturday farmers market.
A few reliable chains and a good grocery store; food is not a priority.

questions.t: Your relationship with coffee and cafes:
o: I need a great independent cafe within walking distance; it is my second living room.
I like a good cafe but will drive to one.
Drip coffee at home is fine.
I do not drink coffee or care about cafes.

questions.t: Which drinks culture appeals most?
o: Craft cocktail bars and natural-wine spots.
Breweries and taprooms with dogs and picnic tables.
Front-porch sweet tea or a cold beer with neighbors.
I do not drink alcohol, and I prefer places where that is normal and easy.

questions.t: Dietary life: which is closest to you?
o: Vegan or vegetarian, and I want plenty of options.
I eat everything but care about local and organic sourcing.
Specific religious or cultural dietary practices (kosher, halal, and so on) that I want to keep easily.

questions.t: A food you could not live without nearby:
o: Fresh seafood straight off the boat.
Real barbecue or Southern home cooking.
Authentic Mexican or Southwestern food with green chile.

questions.t: "I would happily drive 45 minutes for an exceptional meal."
Your favorite way to spend a free Saturday morning:
o: A trail run, mountain bike ride, or paddle.
A gallery, museum, or bookstore crawl.
Fixing something in the garage or garden.
Brunch with friends in a lively neighborhood.
Worship service, volunteering, or community work.

questions.t: Which hobby are you most likely to pick up next?
o: Woodworking, welding, or building a 3D printer.

questions.t: Your ideal vacation:
o: Exploring a great city's museums, food, and neighborhoods.
A quiet cabin by a lake.
A cultural heritage trip: historic towns, battlefields, cathedrals.

questions.t: How do you feel about team sports, as a fan?
o: I live and die with my teams; game day is sacred.
I follow a team casually and enjoy going to games.
I will watch the big games for the social side.
I do not care about sports.

questions.t: Which would you rather do on a weeknight?
o: A church small group, choir practice, or study circle.
Work on a personal project at home.

questions.t: Your relationship with animals:
o: I want room for dogs, maybe horses or livestock.
A dog or cat, and a dog-friendly neighborhood matters.
Pets are nice but not a factor.
I prefer not to have pets.

questions.t: "I would rather spend a weekend outdoors than in any city."
Collecting, tinkering, and DIY projects:
o: Central to my life; I need a workshop or studio space.

questions.t: A friend offers you a free weekend lesson. Which do you grab?
o: A ballroom or salsa dance class.

questions.t: Your relationship with shopping:
o: I love strolling boutiques and vintage shops on a walkable main street.
A big mall or outlet center is fun.
I buy as little as possible and fix what I own.

questions.t: Games and puzzles:
o: Board-game cafes and trivia leagues are my scene.
A weekly card game with the same friends for years.
Video games online with friends anywhere.

questions.t: "I would happily spend every weekend working on my house and yard."
Your ideal live-entertainment night:
o: A sweaty indie or punk show in a small club.
A country, bluegrass, or gospel concert.
A big stadium show or festival.

questions.t: How often do you want to go out to cultural events (shows, exhibits, readings)?
Which music best fits your soul?
Your ideal movie theater:
o: An art-house cinema showing foreign films and restored classics.

questions.t: Which of these festivals would you travel for?
o: A music festival in the desert or mountains.
A county fair with livestock shows and a demolition derby.
A Pride celebration or cultural heritage parade.

questions.t: "Living somewhere with a thriving arts scene is essential to my happiness."
Nightlife preference:
o: Bars and clubs open until 2 a.m. or later, within walking distance.
A few good bars and a music venue nearby.
A quiet pub or restaurant that closes by 10.
No nightlife needed; I am asleep by 10.

questions.t: Your stance on screens and entertainment at home:
o: I would rather go out than stay in.
Mostly home, often without screens: books, crafts, the garden.

questions.t: The sound environment you find most soothing:
o: City hum: distant traffic, voices, a siren now and then.
A quiet residential street with birds and an occasional lawnmower.
Wind in the trees and nothing else.

questions.t: Light: how do you feel about gray, overcast days?
o: Tolerable, but I need sunshine regularly.
They make me miserable; I need bright sun most days.

questions.t: Which smell says "home" to you?
o: Creosote after desert rain, or sun-baked sage.
Fresh bread and coffee from the bakery downstairs.
Cut grass and a summer thunderstorm.

questions.t: Crowds on sidewalks and in stores:
o: I avoid them at almost any cost.

questions.t: At night, how dark do you want it outside your bedroom window?
o: Dark, with a few distant lights.

questions.t: Your ideal view from your window:
o: Open fields, desert, or prairie to the horizon.

questions.t: Humidity on your skin:
"I am easily overwhelmed by noise, bright lights, or strong smells."
Which tactile pleasure matters most to you?
o: Cold mountain air in my lungs.
Dry desert sun on my skin.

Early career, building skills and income.

Part-time, gig work, or between jobs.

Hospitality, food service, retail, or tourism.

A mid-sized city with a strong young-professional scene.

Generous; location matters more than price.

I do not think about taxes when choosing where to live.

Funding experiences, travel, and a rich life.

Regularly at a gym, studio, or class.

o: Yoga studios, meditation centers, and juice bars.
Church potlucks and Sunday dinners; wellness is community.

Often: errands, coffee, and dinner on foot.

Not much; a basic clinic is enough.

None, and I prefer sober-friendly environments.

o: Sunshine and warmth for joints and mood.
Easy access to gyms, pools, and fitness studios.
None in particular, or prefer not to say.

questions.t: Your relationship with a car right now:
o: I do not own one and do not want to.

Curiosity and openness to new ideas.
Fairness and equal opportunity for all.

A broad public effort, state or federal, tackles root causes.

Society generally improves when we challenge old norms.

Expansive: guarantees like universal healthcare and housing.

Rare; I would prefer few guns around.

Keep it small and rural; resist sprawl and towers alike.

A slow family day, with shops open.
Brunch and errands, just another weekend day.
A late-night recovery day after Saturday.

Expanding arts, language, and inclusive programs.
Funding equity across rich and poor districts.
Prefer not to say, or none.

questions.t: "I prefer to live where people value privacy and mind their own business."

An immigrant or refugee resettlement program.
A public library or arts nonprofit.

How do you feel about being around people who live very differently from you (culturally, economically, in values)?
o: I seek it out; it is why I would choose a place.
I prefer people who share my background and way of life.

questions.t: Your view of wealth:

Fine, as long as it is earned honestly.
Often a product of luck and circumstance.
A structural problem when it concentrates.

o: "Come back with a warrant." (said with a grin)

questions.t: How important is it to live near a congregation of your specific tradition (a particular church, synagogue, mosque, temple, or meetinghouse)?
A neighborhood where faith is very visible (churches on every corner, prayer at public events, religious schools):

questions.t: Which spiritual practices are part of your life?
o: Alternative spirituality: astrology, energy work, crystals, and the like.
None, or prefer not to say.

questions.t: Would you like your social life to be organized around a faith community?
o: Yes; it is the center of my relationships.

questions.t: Interfaith and religious diversity in a community feels:

Less important than a strong shared faith.

questions.t: "My ideal community has a strong moral and religious foundation."
Where does your sense of meaning mostly come from?
When you are overwhelmed, your body's first signal is usually:
o: Irritability; small things set me off.
Tension: headaches, a tight jaw, a knotted stomach.

questions.t: Your go-to way to decompress after a terrible day:
o: A hard workout or a long run outdoors.
Drinks or dinner out with friends.
Silence: a dark room, a bath, no screens.
Prayer, meditation, or a spiritual practice.

questions.t: A traffic jam makes you 30 minutes late. You:
o: Get annoyed but use the time to make calls.
Shrug and turn up a podcast.
Rarely face traffic because I chose a life without it.

questions.t: Which environment would most reduce your daily stress?
o: A quiet house with land around it.
A walkable neighborhood where everything is close.
A small town where everyone knows each other.
A place near the ocean or a lake.
A place near mountains or forest trails.

questions.t: "A fast pace of life energizes me rather than stresses me."
Under chronic stress, you are most likely to:
o: Seek out friends and talk it through.
Escape into games, shows, or books.

questions.t: Weather affects your mood:
o: Enormously; gray winters drag me down.
I actually love dramatic weather: storms, blizzards, heat waves.

questions.t: If you could remove one stressor from your life forever, it would be:
A neighbor's dog barks every night until midnight. You:
o: Knock on their door and talk it out that week.
Endure it and complain to friends.
Call the HOA, landlord, or city.
Start looking for a place with more distance between houses.

questions.t: In a disagreement with a close friend, you:
o: Wait until emotions cool, then talk.
Drop hints and hope they notice.
Let it go to preserve the friendship.

o: Love it; I always know where I stand.
Prefer a culture of gentle manners and indirect kindness.

questions.t: A coworker takes credit for your work in a meeting. You:
o: Correct the record on the spot.
Let it slide and quietly protect my work in the future.

questions.t: When a local controversy erupts (a new development, a school policy), you:
o: Show up at the town meeting and speak.
Write a letter or post a thoughtful comment.
Discuss it with friends but stay out publicly.

After an argument, you recover:
o: Slowly; I replay it for a long time.

o: Take charge and direct people to exits.
Look to others to see whether it is real.
Feel a spike of panic but get out fast.

o: Decide in an hour, using gut instinct.
Make a pros-and-cons list and decide by evening.
Call everyone I trust for advice.
Ask for an extension; I cannot decide that fast.

questions.t: In an emergency, people expect you to be:
o: The researcher who knows what to do.

questions.t: When stakes are high, you trust:

o: Sign the dream apartment; life is short.
Lean toward the dream but negotiate.
Take the cheaper one; money saved is freedom earned.

questions.t: Which statement about risk fits you?
o: I avoid risk wherever I can.

questions.t: A hurricane, wildfire, blizzard, or tornado warning is issued for your area. Which would you find most tolerable as a recurring possibility where you live?

When life gets hard, the support system you lean on most is:
o: A therapist, support group, or professional.

questions.t: A burnout recovery month would look like:

Staying in the city but taking classes and seeing friends.
A mountain town with daily hikes.

questions.t: Being near a major hospital, police presence, and services makes you feel:

questions.t: Your relationship with routine during stressful times:

I break it to shake things up.

Podcasts and newsletters from independent voices.

questions.t: How do you feel about places where internet and cell service are spotty?

questions.t: Talking with locals while traveling, you most enjoy hearing about:

questions.t: "I like being around people who challenge my views."

o: A community church or interfaith center.

A truck or car for everything.

questions.t: Noise level you can comfortably sleep through:

questions.t: "I would feel trapped in a place where I had to drive everywhere."

o: Over an hour, if the home and town are worth it.

questions.t: Which "city energy" do you want?

questions.t: Ideal distance from a big city if you do not live in one:
