Hours away; cities are for occasional visits.

questions.t: Elevation gain on your daily walk:
o: Steep hills: I want a workout and views.

questions.t: "I would happily live in a place that is hard to reach if it were beautiful and wild."
Which arts scene would you most want to be part of?
o: A big-city scene: major museums, Broadway-style theater, symphonies.
A gritty, DIY scene: warehouse galleries, zines, house shows.
A small-town arts colony: studios, galleries, and art walks.
A folk and heritage scene: quilting, woodcarving, old-time music.
Arts are not a priority for me.

questions.t: Which music city would you most like to call home?
o: A city of honky-tonks and songwriters' rounds.
A city of jazz clubs, brass bands, and second lines.
A city of indie rock and record stores.
A city with a world-class orchestra and opera.
Music is not a deciding factor.

questions.t: You see a flyer for an open-mic night at a local cafe. You:
o: Might go if friends are going.

questions.t: "I want to live among artists, makers, and eccentrics."
Murals, street art, and quirky public art make a neighborhood feel:
o: Messy; I prefer clean, traditional streetscapes.

questions.t: A community theater production of a classic musical, in a small town, would be:
o: Something I would go to support friends.

questions.t: Which food culture would you join most enthusiastically?
o: A "foodie city" with acclaimed chefs and new openings every week.
A barbecue, crawfish-boil, or church-supper culture.
A farm-to-table, CSA, and farmers-market culture.
A brewery, winery, or distillery region.
Food is not a deciding factor.

questions.t: Your Saturday market of choice:
o: A huge urban market with 100 vendors and global street food.
A small-town farmers market with folk music.
A flea market or antique fair.
A big-box store; markets are not my thing.

questions.t: "A neighborhood without good independent restaurants is not a neighborhood I want."
A startup scene (coworking spaces, pitch nights, venture capital) in your city would be:
o: Essential; I want to build something.
A negative; it brings rising costs and tech culture.

questions.t: Which professional community excites you most?
A "company town" dominated by one big employer (a university, a hospital, a military base, a big manufacturer) feels:
In your ideal town, the local status symbol is:
o: A roof-rack full of skis, bikes, and kayaks.
A big pickup and a bass boat.
A gallery opening in your honor.

questions.t: Which outdoor community would you join?
"I want to live in a place where my neighbors are as obsessed with the outdoors as I am."
A ski town in winter (crowded lifts, fresh powder, apres-ski) sounds:
A beach town in summer (boardwalks, surf shops, tourists, sunsets):
Living in a college town (student energy, football Saturdays, lectures, cheap eats) sounds:
o: Good, if I am not right next to campus.

questions.t: Which campus vibe would feel most like home?
o: An Ivy-style campus with old stone buildings.
A big state school with a massive stadium.
A small liberal-arts college with a quirky arts scene.
A faith-based university with a strong spiritual community.

questions.t: How important is it that your community is racially and ethnically diverse?
How important is a visible LGBTQ+ community (bars, centers, Pride events) where you live?
o: Important; I want inclusion even if I am not personally part of it.
I prefer communities where it is not a focus.

questions.t: Which would you most like to hear spoken around you on a daily walk?
o: English with a strong regional accent.

questions.t: "I want to live somewhere being different is celebrated."
A community with a strong shared ethnic, cultural, or religious heritage (Dutch Reformed towns, Amish country, historic Black neighborhoods, Latino barrios, Jewish enclaves):
o: Very appealing if it is my heritage.
Appealing to experience as a respectful neighbor.
I prefer places without a dominant identity.

questions.t: Your ideal relationship between your town and its churches, temples, or faith institutions:
o: Faith is woven into civic life: prayer at games, church festivals, Sunday closures.
Faith communities are visible and active, but civic life is secular.
Faith is private; I barely notice it.
I would prefer a strongly secular place.

questions.t: Which faith or spiritual scene would you seek out?
o: A large, active congregation with youth programs and small groups.
A historic church, synagogue, or temple with liturgy and tradition.
A meditation center, yoga ashram, or alternative spiritual community.

questions.t: A town known for its spiritual energy, vortexes, and healing retreats sounds:
On a Saturday night at 11 p.m., the ideal sound from your street is:
o: Bass from a club and laughter from a bar patio.
A few voices and a distant band.

questions.t: LGBTQ+ nightlife, drag brunch, and cabaret are:
o: A big part of my social life.

questions.t: "My ideal town is quiet, safe, and a little boring, and I mean that as a compliment."
Which sports culture would you fit best?
o: A big-league city with pro teams in every sport.
A college football town where Saturday is a holy day.
A high school sports town: Friday night lights.
A participation culture: marathons, rec leagues, and races.
I do not care about sports culture.

questions.t: Tailgating, team colors, and rivalries:
A town with a hardware store, a feed store, a makerspace, and a tool library:
o: Is my dream; I build and fix things.

questions.t: Homesteading, backyard chickens, and self-sufficiency:
Craft culture: small-batch everything (coffee roasters, letterpress, leatherworkers, woodworkers):
o: I want to be one of them.
I want to buy from them.

questions.t: A planned active-adult community with golf carts, pickleball courts, clubs, and organized social calendars:
Your ideal age mix in your neighborhood:
Accessible living (flat terrain, single-level homes, nearby medical care, shuttle services) matters:
Which community motto would you most want on your welcome sign?
Which would bother you more?
o: A town that feels culturally homogeneous.
A town that feels like it is losing its traditions.
A town with no outdoor recreation.
A town where housing is unaffordable.

questions.t: How politically mixed would you like your community to be?
o: Leaning my way, with some mix.

questions.t: If you had to pick your community's "personality type," it would be:
Which "third place" (not home, not work) would you want within a few blocks?
o: A dive bar or music venue.
A church hall or community center.
A climbing gym or bike shop.

questions.t: "I would rather be a regular in a small town than anonymous in a big city."
Regular winter snow (snow on the ground for weeks most winters):
o: Dealbreaker; I will not live with regular snow.
I would prefer to avoid it, but it is not a dealbreaker.
I am fine with it or want it.

questions.t: Long stretches of extreme summer heat (frequent 100°F+ days or high heat with humidity):
Humid, sticky summers:
Living within about 20 minutes of an ocean coastline:
Living close to real mountains:
A large airport with extensive nonstop flights within about an hour:
Being able to live comfortably without a car:
Housing and living costs at or below the national average:
o: Must-have; I cannot or will not pay more.

questions.t: A strongly family-oriented community with well-regarded schools and kid-centered amenities:
Genuine quiet at night and low ambient noise:
Which density limit is a must for you?
o: I must live in a genuinely urban neighborhood.
I must live in a small town or rural area.

questions.t: A place where LGBTQ+ people are visibly welcomed and safe:
Faith community requirement:
o: Must-have: I need a place where faith is central to community life.
Must-avoid: I need a strongly secular place where religion is not prominent in civic life.

questions.t: Civic and political climate:
o: Must-have: the local culture must broadly match my own civic outlook.
I prefer a match but can adapt.
Not important; I enjoy a mix.

questions.t: Is there one eastern region you would refuse to live in?
Is there one western region you would refuse to live in?
Which ONE factor matters most in where you live? (Priority #1)
o: City life: density, walkability, arts, and nightlife.

questions.t: Which factor matters SECOND most? (Priority #2; choose a different answer than above)
o: City life: density, walkability, arts, and nightlife.

locations.name: Capitol Hill
locations.desc: Historic heart of Seattle's LGBTQ+ and music scenes; dense, transit-rich, rainy and green, with Cascades and Puget Sound close by.

locations.name: Park Slope
locations.desc: Brownstone blocks beside Prospect Park; famously family-friendly, literary, and progressive, with world-class culture a subway ride away.

locations.name: Mission District
locations.desc: Sunniest corner of San Francisco; historic Latino neighborhood known for murals, taquerias, nightlife, and tech-industry proximity; mild year-round.

locations.name: Logan Square
locations.desc: Boulevards, greystones, and a deep bar, music, and restaurant scene on the Blue Line; real winters and a famously friendly big city.

locations.name: South End
locations.desc: Victorian brick rowhouses, a strong LGBTQ+ history, galleries and restaurants; at the center of Boston's medical, academic, and biotech economy.

locations.name: Fishtown
locations.desc: Former working-class river ward turned music-venue, brewery, and restaurant hub; rowhouses and grit with relatively attainable big-city costs.

locations.name: Hawthorne / Southeast
locations.desc: Bungalows, food carts, vintage shops, and makers; famously quirky and green, with Mount Hood and the Columbia Gorge within reach.

locations.name: Downtown / Mapleton Hill
locations.desc: University town against the Flatirons; elite outdoor-athlete culture, startups, wellness, and very high housing costs; sunny and dry with snowy winters.

locations.name: Downtown / Kerrytown
locations.desc: Classic Big Ten college town with a walkable downtown, farmers market, art fair, and big-time football; four strong seasons.

locations.name: Willy Street / Near East Side
locations.desc: Isthmus neighborhood between two lakes near the state capitol and university; co-ops, bike paths, and a strong farmers-market culture; cold winters.

locations.name: Downtown / Northside
locations.desc: Leafy Southern university town in the Research Triangle; college basketball culture, mild winters, humid summers.

locations.name: West Asheville
locations.desc: Funky Blue Ridge neighborhood with breweries, musicians, and craftspeople; forests, rivers, and trails everywhere; tourism-driven economy.

locations.name: Downtown / Old North End
locations.desc: Lake Champlain city with a pedestrian marketplace, university energy, farm-to-table food, and nearby ski mountains; long snowy winters.

locations.name: Downtown
locations.desc: Fast-growing Montana State University town ringed by mountain ranges and blue-ribbon trout streams; remote-worker magnet with rising costs.

locations.name: Downtown / University District
locations.desc: River-city college town where the Clark Fork runs through downtown; writers, fly-fishers, and a strong local music scene.

locations.name: Old Bend / Downtown
locations.desc: High-desert outdoor mecca on the Deschutes River near Mount Bachelor; breweries, trails, sunshine, and a big remote-work population.

locations.name: Downtown
locations.desc: Historic railroad town on the Animas River in the San Juan Mountains; mountain biking, rafting, and a laid-back small-town feel.

locations.name: Downtown / Southside
locations.desc: High-altitude university town in the world's largest ponderosa pine forest; dark-sky city near the Grand Canyon; snowy winters and mild summers.

locations.name: Downtown / Eastside
locations.desc: Adobe state capital with one of the country's densest gallery scenes, centuries of Pueblo and Hispanic heritage, high-desert light, and green chile.

locations.name: East Austin
locations.desc: Rapidly changing eastside of the "Live Music Capital"; taco trucks, venues, startups, and long hot summers in a progressive city within a traditional-leaning state.

locations.name: East Nashville
locations.desc: Bungalow neighborhood across the river from downtown, home to songwriters, indie musicians, and chef-driven restaurants.

locations.name: Downtown Decatur
locations.desc: Small walkable city inside metro Atlanta with a courthouse square, strong schools, festivals, tree canopy, and proximity to Emory and the CDC.

locations.name: Old Village / Mount Pleasant
locations.desc: Lowcountry suburb across the harbor from Charleston; marshes, beaches, shrimp boats, churches, and family-oriented neighborhoods.

locations.name: Downtown / Old Northeast
locations.desc: Sunny waterfront downtown with murals, museums, a long public waterfront park system, and Gulf beaches nearby; hurricane exposure.

locations.name: The Villages
locations.desc: Vast age-restricted active-adult community with golf-cart travel, town squares with nightly music, and hundreds of clubs.

locations.name: Old Town
locations.desc: Polished desert downtown with galleries, resorts, spring-training baseball, nightlife, and hiking in the McDowell Mountains; very hot summers.

locations.name: Sam Hughes / University
locations.desc: Historic neighborhood by the University of Arizona; saguaro desert, sky-island mountains, Sonoran food heritage, and a relaxed pace.

locations.name: Frisco
locations.desc: Booming master-planned suburb north of Dallas with corporate campuses, top-rated schools, megachurches, and pro-sports facilities.

locations.name: Gilbert
locations.desc: Family-centric East Valley suburb with a large faith community, parks, and a revitalized Heritage District; intensely hot summers.

locations.name: Downtown
locations.desc: Civil War-era Main Street, excellent schools, strong churchgoing culture, and the Christian-music industry; affluent and traditional-leaning.

locations.name: North Provo / BYU area
locations.desc: Home of Brigham Young University beneath the Wasatch; a family-centered, largely Latter-day Saint community with a strong tech corridor and little nightlife.

locations.name: Briargate
locations.desc: North-side family suburb near the Air Force Academy, many national Christian ministries, and Pikes Peak views.

locations.name: Downtown
locations.desc: Moravian-founded Lancaster County town with a charming Main Street, pretzel and chocolate heritage, and surrounding Plain-community farmland.

locations.name: Downtown
locations.desc: Dutch-heritage Lake Michigan city with a heated-sidewalk downtown, Tulip Time festival, many churches, and Hope College.

locations.name: Downtown
locations.desc: Friendly, affordable prairie city with a waterfall park downtown, big healthcare and banking employers, and no state income tax.

locations.name: East Village
locations.desc: Walkable district below the state capitol with boutiques, bars, and a huge Saturday farmers market; insurance-industry economy and low costs.

locations.name: Dundee
locations.desc: Leafy, historic streetcar neighborhood with a small commercial strip; stable Midwestern city with major finance and insurance employers.

locations.name: German Village
locations.desc: Brick streets and restored 19th-century cottages near downtown in a growing state capital and Big Ten city.

locations.name: Lawrenceville
locations.desc: Revived rowhouse district along the Allegheny with galleries, bars, robotics firms, and hospitals; hilly, affordable for a real city.

locations.name: Lyn-Lake / Uptown
locations.desc: Near the Chain of Lakes with year-round trails, theaters, and music venues; deep cold winters and a strong civic culture.

locations.name: Brookside
locations.desc: Tudor-and-bungalow neighborhood with a 1920s shopping district; barbecue, jazz heritage, and passionate sports fans.

locations.name: The Highlands
locations.desc: Bardstown Road's eclectic strip of bars, restaurants, and Victorian homes near Cherokee Park; bourbon culture and moderate costs.

locations.name: North Shore
locations.desc: Walkable riverfront district across the Tennessee River from downtown; climbing, paddling, and trails within minutes; city-wide fiber internet.

locations.name: Downtown
locations.desc: Celebrated walkable Main Street with a waterfall park and suspension bridge; manufacturing economy, Blue Ridge foothills, strong church culture.

locations.name: Downtown / Dickson Street
locations.desc: University of Arkansas town in the Ozarks with a nightlife strip, mountain-bike trails, and a regional economy anchored by large corporate HQs.

locations.name: The Square
locations.desc: Literary Southern town around a courthouse square and independent bookstore; Ole Miss football Saturdays and gracious traditions.

locations.name: Bywater / Marigny
locations.desc: Colorful Creole cottages, brass bands, artists, and festivals downriver from the French Quarter; hot, humid, and hurricane-exposed.

locations.name: Historic District
locations.desc: Live-oak squares, antebellum architecture, a major art-and-design college, and a relaxed walkable core near the coast.

locations.name: Kaimuki
locations.desc: Local-favorite neighborhood behind Diamond Head with family restaurants and bakeries; ocean and ridge trails minutes away; extremely high costs.

locations.name: North Park
locations.desc: Craft-beer and restaurant hub near Balboa Park with near-perfect weather and beaches 15 to 20 minutes away.

locations.name: Silver Lake
locations.desc: Hillside creative-class neighborhood around a reservoir; musicians, designers, cafes, and the entertainment industry.

locations.name: Downtown / Movie Colony
locations.desc: Midcentury-modern desert resort city beneath the San Jacinto Mountains; a major LGBTQ+ and retiree destination with scorching summers.

locations.name: Uptown / West Sedona
locations.desc: Red-rock canyon town known for hiking, galleries, and New Age retreats and "vortexes"; tourism-heavy and pricey.

locations.name: Town of Jackson
locations.desc: Western town square at the gateway to Grand Teton and Yellowstone; world-class skiing and wildlife; among the most expensive housing markets in the U.S.

locations.name: Munjoy Hill
locations.desc: Hilltop peninsula neighborhood above Casco Bay; lobster boats, an acclaimed small-city food scene, and long snowy winters.

locations.name: Downtown / Fall Creek
locations.desc: Gorges, waterfalls, and Cayuga Lake around two universities; co-ops, farms, and a famously progressive small-city culture.

locations.name: Capitol Hill
locations.desc: Rowhouse neighborhood steps from the Capitol and Eastern Market; policy careers, free national museums, and a fast professional pace.

locations.name: North End
locations.desc: Tree-lined historic neighborhood with direct foothill trail access, the Boise River greenbelt, and a nearby ski hill; friendly and growing.

locations.name: Downtown
locations.desc: Preserved 19th-century river town in the hilly Driftless region with antique shops, inns, and quiet, scenic countryside.

locations.name: Marfa
locations.desc: Tiny high-desert town in far West Texas famous for minimalist art installations, enormous skies, and isolation; hours from a major airport.

locations.name: Main Street
locations.desc: German-heritage Hill Country town with wineries, peach orchards, churches, and a busy Main Street; conservative and close-knit.

locations.name: Berlin (Holmes County)
locations.desc: Heart of one of the largest Amish and Mennonite communities in the world; rolling farmland, furniture makers, and very quiet nights.

locations.name: Highlands
locations.desc: Walkable restaurant-and-bar neighborhood with skyline views and the Rockies about an hour west; sunny, dry, and active.

locations.name: Montrose
locations.desc: Eclectic inner-loop district near the Menil Collection and Museum District; historic LGBTQ+ hub in one of the most diverse U.S. cities; humid and hurricane-exposed.

locations.name: Alamo Heights
locations.desc: Established small city within San Antonio with strong schools and churches; Tex-Mex heritage, military community, and hot summers.

locations.name: Downtown
locations.desc: Corporate headquarters town with a major American-art museum, hundreds of miles of mountain-bike trails, and family-friendly neighborhoods.

locations.name: Clarendon
locations.desc: Metro-served high-rise and townhouse district minutes from Washington; young professionals, government and defense-tech careers.

locations.name: Viroqua
locations.desc: Driftless Area town known for organic farming, a large food co-op, Waldorf education, and neighboring Amish farms; deep rural quiet.

locations.name: Floyd
locations.desc: Blue Ridge Plateau hamlet famous for its Friday-night old-time jamboree, back-to-the-land homesteaders, and artisans alongside longtime farm families.

locations.name: Downtown
locations.desc: Resort city on a large mountain lake in the Idaho Panhandle; boating, skiing, and a strongly traditional-leaning political culture.

locations.name: Hoboken
locations.desc: Square-mile brownstone city on the Hudson facing Manhattan; young professionals, bars, and a quick commute to Wall Street and Midtown.

locations.name: Carmel
locations.desc: Affluent planned suburb with roundabouts, a performing-arts center, the Monon Trail, and top schools; orderly and family-oriented.

locations.name: Old Town
locations.desc: Subtropical island at the end of the Overseas Highway; bike-friendly lanes, a famously live-and-let-live culture, nightlife, and serious hurricane exposure.
